title: Lombardelli explains why weak hiring has yet to dislodge her case for another rise
summary: Clare Lombardelli saw a case for a further near-term increase in Bank Rate unless evidence emerged that inflationary pressure was weakening. Her reason was partly who had become unemployed. Firms had cut recruitment while retaining experienced staff. Many jobseekers were young and looking in industries where vacancies had fallen furthest. If those people could not readily fill openings elsewhere, rising unemployment would exert less downward pressure on wages. This was the Deputy Governor’s judgment on November 10. The collective decision she cited was the preceding week’s 8–1 vote to raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4%.

Unemployment rose from below 4% in 2022 to above 5% late in 2025, then fell to 4.7% in the three months to August. It stayed around 5% in the November central projection. Output was stronger and unemployment lower than in the middle of three April scenarios, when the Bank had issued no central projection. Redundancies remained near their pre-pandemic rate while vacancies fell below theirs. Chart 5 attributes most of the recent rise in unemployment to slower job finding. It infers hiring and separations from the duration of unemployment, and the underlying Labour Force Survey has measurement issues. Vacancy surveys and redundancy notifications point in the same direction.

Why hold on to employees as demand weakens? Managers who struggled to recruit after the pandemic valued their existing staff. With energy costs rising, many scaled back hiring and accepted lower margins. Bank contacts planned to recover margins through higher prices and savings on procurement or through automation. Chart 9 shows the balance of firms reporting a change, so it cannot quantify aggregate margin compression. If high costs persist, employers may cut existing jobs, weakening household demand and altering the inflation outlook.

A longer-running decline in mobility makes sector differences matter. More than 3% of employees switched jobs each quarter around thirty years ago, against a little over 2% recently. Moves across industry boundaries also became less frequent. Still, almost three million job switches occurred in 2025, with people who moved more than once contributing multiple switches. Those aged 16–24 were about one eighth of the labour force but accounted for more than half the increase in unemployment since mid-2022. Vacancies were 14% below pre-pandemic levels overall, 19% lower in accommodation and food and 46% lower in retail. These last two industries regularly provide first jobs. Chart 17 assigns first-time jobseekers to likely industries using earlier entry patterns, so the size of the mismatch is estimated.

Some employers also faced higher relative minimum wages for young people. Among firms affected by the National Living Wage, 29% said they would reduce overall employment, a stated intention about jobs of all ages. Missing a first job can delay the acquisition of skills. Better matching can also lift a switcher’s pay and productivity together. Although improved recruitment could explain some of the decline in short-lived jobs, weaker reported satisfaction and fewer opportunities to progress weigh against that benign interpretation. The Bank judged underlying pay growth near the upper end of the range consistent with the inflation target. Lombardelli still saw insufficient evidence that equilibrium unemployment had changed materially.

New technology gives that distinction a practical test. From January to August, industries used by the Bank as a proxy for AI activity contributed about 0.5 percentage points to gross value added growth. Their contribution above its usual level was about 0.3 points, just under one fifth of aggregate growth. The proxy includes unrelated activity and omits some construction and research. Faster productivity growth could support incomes with less inflation. If entry-level tasks disappear before training and new roles arrive, unemployment could rise with little initial relief for prices.

Table A explains why she favoured gradual policy decisions. Direct increases in fuel and utility prices typically operate within a year. Supply-chain pass-through can develop over two years. Wage bargaining and inflation expectations can prolong pressure for up to three years, while lost purchasing power can depress demand over a similar period. Relative to July the energy shock was larger and more persistent. Indirect effects were still limited, evidence of second-round effects was inconclusive, and household spending and business activity had held up better than she expected. The smaller demand offset strengthened her case for another rise. Broader wage disinflation or a sharper spending slowdown would weaken it.

questions.question: Is a given rise in unemployment now buying less wage disinflation because of mismatch?
questions.detail: Track the subsequent growth of settlements, regular private pay and firms’ own wage expectations alongside job-finding and separation rates. Compare industries where vacancies remained elevated with retail and other entry-intensive sectors, allowing for their different energy exposure and initial wage trends. Aggregate unemployment rising while sector-specific hiring difficulties and pay persist would strengthen the mismatch explanation. If pay weakens across sectors as vacancies fall, ordinary cyclical demand weakness could account for much of the evidence.

questions.question: When does absorbing energy costs in margins give way to layoffs or price increases?
questions.detail: Use repeated business-survey answers and Agents’ evidence to distinguish higher selling prices, efficiency savings and lower employment. Trace the sequence from restrained hiring to possible redundancies and compare energy-intensive and less exposed employers. A decline in sales with unchanged pricing and greater actual layoffs would strengthen the speech’s downside scenario. A larger reported energy bill alongside recovering margins and rising selling prices would instead point towards the indirect inflation channel.

questions.question: How much of the decline in youth entry reflects the absence of starter jobs rather than a lasting fall in capacity?
questions.detail: Match vacancy and first-hire data by sector, locality and age, maintaining consistent definitions across the pandemic and occupational reclassifications. Observe whether hiring resumes as sectoral demand recovers, and whether young entrants then move into ordinary progression and wage paths. Persistently lower employment and pay after comparable vacancies return would be more consistent with skill loss or matching frictions. Track the uncertainty around assigning industries to people who have never worked.

questions.question: Would more resilient activity justify a further rise if the composition of that activity changes?
questions.detail: Reassess her four channels jointly using the energy path, realised indirect price changes, settlements and household spending that were observable before the next decision. If a disproportionate share of additional output comes from higher productive capacity rather than demand for constrained resources, headline activity alone overstates the policy implication. Conversely, resilient demand, slower wage disinflation and firmer pricing expectations would fit her conditional case even without another jump in headline energy prices.

limitation: The forward policy judgment belongs to Clare Lombardelli. The speech’s flow decomposition, counterfactual scenarios and AI sector proxy are estimated quantities. The charts and tables do not identify a causal wage or market-price effect.
